summary: Candidate A is meaningfully preferable because it verifies multipart content and end-to-end replay after a 429, while B barely tests the uploaded payload and does not exercise Upload retries. However, both patches violate the explicit requirement to route Upload through FilesService.Add.
reasons: A verifies the multipart field name, uploaded filename, and exact file contents; B never reads or asserts the part content.

A exercises FilesService.Upload across a 429 and confirms the complete multipart body survives the retry. B only adds a generic bytes.Reader transport test and does not verify the retried request body.
A provides clearer, distinct validation errors for an empty filename and nil content, whereas B collapses both cases into one message.
A documents the new convenience API and the replayability distinction while preserving Add's signature and implementation behavior.
risks_a: Upload duplicates Add's option processing, request construction, response decoding, and missing-data error instead of calling s.Add(ctx, body, contentType, opts...), directly violating the frozen contract and creating future drift risk.
The retry test does not set RetryAllMethods: true, so it does not faithfully model the reported POST-retry configuration.
There are no explicit tests for empty filename, nil content, or source-reader failures, despite the required test coverage.
risks_b: Upload duplicates Add's machinery rather than routing through Add, directly violating the frozen contract.
The multipart test does not verify uploaded content.

There is no Upload-level retry test; the generic transport test does not establish that Upload produces a replayable multipart request or that content survives replay onto the second request body—it does not read either request body at all (and also mutates calls unsafely in a parallel test if RoundTrip behavior ever becomes concurrent). There are also no validation or source-reader-error tests.
